expectedText:
SPERM/EGG DONOR PARENTAGE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

SPERM/EGG/EMBRYO DONOR PARENTAGE — FACTS DECLARATION
This information sheet concerns assisted reproduction described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613, involving Jordan LeePat Morgan (the intended parent or parents) and Taylor Morgan (the donor). The parties state, for purposes of the statutory framework described in this document, the following facts about the donation: Anonymous sperm donation through a licensed sperm bank.

This information sheet records these facts as stated by the parties; it does not itself determine whether Taylor Morgan is, or is not, treated in law as a parent of any child conceived, and it does not itself determine whether Pat Morgan — if applicable — is treated in law as a parent. Those outcomes depend on which provision of Cal. Fam. Code § 7613 applies to the facts as they actually occurred, including whether the donated material was provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or a licensed sperm bank, and whether, and when, any written or oral agreement about parentage was made.

This information sheet is not itself a written agreement under Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(a), (b), (c), or (d), and does not itself satisfy any writing requirement described in this document unless it independently meets the content and signature elements those provisions require.

THE SPERM DONOR'S OWN PARENTAGE — TWO DIFFERENT DEFAULT RULES DEPENDING ON HOW THE SEMEN WAS PROVIDED
Family Code § 7613(b) does not impose one single rule for a semen donor; it sets up two different default outcomes depending on how the semen reached the woman who conceives, and each default can be overcome in a different way. Under § 7613(b)(1), if the semen was "provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or to a licensed sperm bank" for use in assisted reproduction by a woman other than the donor's spouse, the donor is treated by default as if the donor is not the natural parent of any child conceived — and that default only flips if the donor and the woman signed a written agreement, before conception, that the donor would be a parent. Under § 7613(b)(2), if the semen was not provided through a licensed physician or sperm bank in that way — the more informal, "known donor" fact pattern — the default runs the other direction by negative implication of the statute's own conditional structure: the donor is treated as not the natural parent only "if either of the following are met": (A) the donor and the woman signed a written agreement, before conception, that the donor would not be a parent, or (B) a court finds by clear and convincing evidence that, before conception, the woman and the donor had an oral agreement that the donor would not be a parent. Neither pathway in current law makes physician involvement a universal precondition to a donor's non-parent status — a donation made outside a licensed physician's or sperm bank's involvement can still result in the donor not being treated as a parent, but only through one of the two mechanisms listed in § 7613(b)(2), and with the practical default running toward the donor being a parent absent one of those mechanisms, rather than away from it as under § 7613(b)(1).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) (1) The donor of semen provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or to a licensed sperm bank for use in assisted reproduction by a woman other than the donor’s spouse is treated in law as if the donor is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived, unless the donor and the woman signed a written agreement before the conception of the child, that the donor would be a parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), semen provided to a licensed physician/surgeon or licensed sperm bank (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  "(2) If the semen is not provided to a licensed physician and surgeon or a licensed sperm bank as specified in paragraph (1), the donor of semen for use in assisted reproduction by a woman other than the donor’s spouse
is treated in law as if the donor is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived if either of the following are met:(A) The donor and the woman signed a written agreement before conception that the donor would not be a parent.(B) A court finds by clear and convincing evidence that the child was conceived through assisted reproduction and that, prior to the conception of the child, the woman and the donor had an oral agreement that the donor would not be a parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), semen not provided through a licensed physician/surgeon or sperm bank (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific donation, nor that every state draws this same physician/non-physician distinction or assigns these same defaults. This clause cites two paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, Family Code § 7613(b)(1) and § 7613(b)(2), both part of the same statutory section verified from a single fetch of that section's full text — they are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the two-default structure is stated directly from the current statutory text, which is the version amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 851, Sec. 5 (AB 1650), effective January 1, 2024, as shown at the end of the fetched section text — this clause does not rely on, and readers should not assume it reflects, any older (e.g., 1990s-era) version of § 7613 that may have imposed a categorical licensed-physician requirement without the alternative pathway described here. Separately, this clause corrects a framing this research started with: the statutory text found here never uses the words "anonymous" or "known" to describe a donor, and draws no distinction under those labels; the physician/sperm-bank-versus-not distinction in § 7613(b)(1)-(2) is a functional analog to what is sometimes informally called an anonymous-donor versus known-donor arrangement, but that is this document's own description of the practical effect, not language the statute itself uses.

THE OVA PROVIDER'S AND EMBRYO PROVIDER'S OWN PARENTAGE — A DIFFERENT RULE THAN THE SEMEN-DONOR RULE
Family Code § 7613 treats a provider of ova, and a provider of a pre-existing embryo, differently from how it treats a semen donor under § 7613(b) — both in what triggers the default non-parent outcome and in the standard used to overcome it. Under § 7613(c), "a person providing ova for use in assisted reproduction by a person other than the provider's spouse or nonmarital partner is treated in law as if the provider is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived unless the court finds satisfactory evidence that the provider of the ova, and each recipient, intended for that provider to have parental rights." Under § 7613(d)(1), the same non-parent default applies to "a provider of an embryo for use in assisted reproduction to an intended parent who is not the provider's spouse or nonmarital partner," rebuttable only if the court finds satisfactory evidence that the provider and the intended parent intended for the provider to be a parent. Neither § 7613(c) nor § 7613(d)(1) conditions the ova or embryo provider's non-parent default on the material having passed through a licensed physician, surgeon, or bank — that physician/bank distinction appears only in § 7613(b)'s semen-donor rule, not here. The two provisions also use a different evidentiary phrase — "satisfactory evidence" of shared intent that the provider have parental rights — than the "clear and convincing evidence" of a prior oral non-parent agreement used as the fallback path in § 7613(b)(2)(B) and in § 7613(a)(2)'s intended-parent-consent rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(c) A person providing ova for use in assisted reproduction by a person other than the provider’s spouse or nonmarital partner is treated in law as if the provider is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived unless the court finds satisfactory
evidence that the provider of the ova, and each recipient, intended for that provider to have parental rights."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(c) (California Legislative Information text), ova provider's default non-parent status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  "(d) (1) A provider of an embryo for use in assisted reproduction to an intended parent who is not the provider’s spouse or nonmarital partner is treated in law as if the provider is not the natural parent of a child thereby conceived unless the court finds satisfactory evidence that the provider and the intended parent intended for the provider to be a parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), embryo provider's default non-parent status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)

This clause cites Family Code § 7613(c) and § 7613(d)(1), two subdivisions of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the comparison to § 7613(b) and the different evidentiary phrasing ("satisfactory evidence" versus "clear and convincing evidence") are stated directly from the statutory text of the section as a whole. This clause corrects a framing this research started with: an assumption that egg/ova donation is governed by the same licensed-physician-or-bank distinction that applies to semen donation under § 7613(b) is not supported by the text found here — § 7613(c) and § 7613(d)(1) contain no such distinction.

THE OTHER (NON-BIRTH-GIVING) INTENDED PARENT'S OWN PARENTAGE — ESTABLISHED BY CONSENT, NOT GENETICS
Family Code § 7613 also addresses, within its own text, the parentage of the intended parent who is not the donor and not the person who conceives and gives birth. Under § 7613(a)(1), if a woman conceives through assisted reproduction using semen or ova, or both, donated by a donor who is not the woman's spouse, and does so "with the consent of another intended parent," that other intended parent "is treated in law as if that intended parent is the natural parent of a child thereby conceived." That consent "shall be in writing and signed by the other intended parent and the woman conceiving through assisted reproduction." Under § 7613(a)(2), the absence of a signed writing does not automatically defeat that intended parent's status: a court may still find the intended parent consented if it finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that before conception the woman and the intended parent had an oral agreement that both would be parents of the child. Nothing in the text of § 7613(a) conditions this outcome on the parties' marital status, on the intended parent's or woman's sex or gender, or on the involvement of a licensed physician.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) (1) If a woman conceives through assisted reproduction with semen or ova or both donated by a donor who is not the woman’s spouse, with the consent of another intended parent, that intended parent is treated in law as if that intended parent is the natural parent of a child thereby conceived. The other intended parent’s consent shall be in writing and signed by the other intended parent and the woman conceiving through assisted reproduction."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), consenting intended parent treated as natural parent; written, signed consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  "(2) Failure to consent in writing, as required by paragraph (1), does not preclude the court from finding that the intended parent consented if the court finds by clear and convincing evidence that, prior to the
conception of the child, the woman and the intended parent had an oral agreement that the woman and the intended parent would both be parents of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), unwritten consent may still be found by clear and convincing evidence of a prior oral agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state extends parentage to a non-genetic, non-birth-giving intended parent on these same consent-based terms. This clause cites Family Code § 7613(a)(1) and § 7613(a)(2), two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the rule is stated directly from statutory text. This directly answers the research question of whether a person who is not the donor, but who intends to be a parent via assisted reproduction, has their own parentage addressed by § 7613 itself: it does, within § 7613(a), rather than requiring resort to a separate companion section. A separate section, § 7613.5, does exist and is addressed in a companion clause of this document, but § 7613.5 provides optional forms to help satisfy § 7613(a)'s own writing requirement — it does not itself impose a different or additional substantive rule about this intended parent's parentage.

OPTIONAL STATUTORY FORMS UNDER § 7613.5, AND HOW THIS FRAMEWORK RELATES TO THE GESTATIONAL CARRIER STATUTE
Family Code § 7613.5 is a separate, companion statutory section that supplies optional fill-in forms for use alongside § 7613, not a different substantive parentage rule. Section 7613.5(a) states that "an intended parent may, but is not required to, use the forms set forth in this section to demonstrate the intent to be a legal parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction," and that "these forms shall satisfy the writing requirement specified in Section 7613," while also making clear that the forms "do not affect any presumptions of parentage based on Section 7611, and do not preclude a court from considering any other claims to parentage under California statute or case law." Section 7613.5(d) confirms use of these particular forms is optional: "this section does not require the use of one of these forms to satisfy the writing requirement of Section 7613" — a different written agreement can also satisfy § 7613's own writing elements. Critically for how this framework relates to this corpus's separate Gestational Carrier (Surrogacy) Agreement Information Sheet, § 7613.5(c) states directly that "these forms do not apply to assisted reproduction agreements for gestational carriers or surrogacy agreements." Sections 7613 and 7613.5 (governing a donor or genetic-material provider's own parentage, and an intended parent's consent-based parentage, outside a gestational-carrier arrangement) and Family Code §§ 7960-7962 (governing an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers specifically) are two distinct, parallel statutory frameworks within the same Uniform Parentage Act part of the Family Code, addressing different fact patterns: this framework does not itself impose, and its text does not cross-reference, the independent-counsel, notarization-or-witnessing, or pre-embryo-transfer-execution requirements that § 7962 imposes specifically on gestational carrier agreements, and conversely the optional § 7613.5 forms are, by their own terms, unusable for a gestational carrier or surrogacy agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) An intended parent may, but is not required to, use the forms set forth in this section to demonstrate the intent to be a legal parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction. These forms shall satisfy the writing requirement specified in Section 7613, and are designed to provide clarity regarding the intentions, at the time of conception, of intended parents using assisted reproduction. These forms do not affect any presumptions of parentage based on Section 7611, and do not preclude a court from considering any other claims to parentage under California statute or case law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), optional forms, satisfy § 7613's writing requirement, do not displace other parentage claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.5.)
  "(c) These forms do not apply to assisted reproduction agreements for gestational carriers or surrogacy agreements."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), forms do not apply to gestational carrier or surrogacy agreements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.5.)
  "(d) This section does not require the use of one of these forms to satisfy the writing requirement of Section 7613."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), use of these particular forms is not mandatory (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text and of how its own two frameworks relate to each other as the statute itself states that relationship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state maintains separate donor-parentage and gestational-carrier statutes, or relates them the same way. This clause cites Family Code § 7613.5(a), § 7613.5(c), and § 7613.5(d), three subdivisions of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent; the separately verified § 7613 text and this corpus's already-verified §§ 7960-7962 gestational-carrier clauses are used here only to state the textual relationship between the frameworks (each framework's own text disclaims coverage of the other), not as newly re-verified citations in this clause. No case law was researched for this clause; the relationship between the two frameworks is stated directly from each statute's own text.

WHEN GENETIC MATERIAL PASSED THROUGH MULTIPLE HANDS, AND EMBRYO-DISPOSITION RENUNCIATION AGREEMENTS BETWEEN CO-OWNERS
Family Code § 7613 addresses two further, more specific situations beyond the core donor and provider rules described elsewhere in this document. First, § 7613(d)(2) addresses a chain-of-custody problem: "if the provider of ova, semen, or embryos is not the original source of the ova or sperm, each original provider's written consent to the donation is required unless that person has executed a writing to consent to the donation, or to waive or relinquish their right to the genetic material, or as otherwise ordered by a court of law." Second, § 7613(e) addresses a written renunciation agreement between two people who jointly control the disposition of stored embryos. Under § 7613(e)(1), if those two people "are not married to one another," they may enter a written agreement in which one of them "renounces all legal interest in the embryos, with the specific intent that the person renouncing all legal interest shall not be a legal parent of any child conceived with use of the embryos," and once that renunciation is signed by everyone with a legal interest in or control over the embryos, "the renouncing person shall be treated in law as a donor, and not a legal parent"; either party may then file the agreement with the court for "an order establishing the nonparentage of the donor." Under § 7613(e)(2), if the two people sharing control of the embryos are instead married to one another at the time they sign such an agreement, it does not become legally binding until "the court's entry of a final decree of dissolution that incorporates the agreement," after which specified marital-presumption provisions (Family Code § 7540, and § 7611(a)-(c)) no longer apply.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(2) If the provider of ova, semen, or embryos is not the original source of the ova or sperm, each original provider’s written consent to the donation is required unless that person has executed a writing to consent to the donation, or to waive or relinquish their right to the genetic material,
or as otherwise ordered by a court of law."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), original genetic-material source's consent required if provider is not the original source (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  "(e) (1) Notwithstanding any other law, persons who are not married to one another and who share legal control over the disposition of embryos shall not be prevented from entering into a written agreement whereby one person renounces all legal interest in the embryos, with the specific intent that the person renouncing all legal interest shall not be a legal parent of any child conceived with use of the embryos, despite any prior oral or written agreements, or legal judgments to the contrary. After that interest has been renounced in a writing signed by all persons with legal interest in or control over disposition of the embryos, the renouncing person shall be treated in law as a donor, and not a legal parent. Upon execution of that agreement, the person who retains legal
interest in and control over disposition of the embryos shall have the sole right to determine the use and disposition of the embryos, including the right to attempt conception of a child, subject to any limitation pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (d). Either party may file the agreement with the court, and the court shall issue an order establishing the nonparentage of the donor."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), unmarried co-owners' written renunciation agreement; renouncing party treated as a donor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  "(2) If persons who share legal control over and interest in one or more embryos are married to one another at the time of signing the agreement, the agreement shall only become legally binding upon the court’s entry of a final decree of dissolution that incorporates the agreement, after which the presumptions pursuant to Section 7540 or subdivisions (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611 shall not apply."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7613(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text), if co-owners are married when signing, agreement binds only upon incorporation into a dissolution decree (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7613.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state has a comparable rule for multi-hand genetic material or embryo-disposition renunciation agreements. This clause cites Family Code § 7613(d)(2) and § 7613(e)(1)-(2), all part of the same statutory section fetched together as one document — treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; both rules are stated directly from statutory text. This clause deliberately covers a narrower topic than a general framework for resolving a contested embryo-disposition dispute: § 7613(e) addresses only a written renunciation agreement voluntarily entered between people who already share legal control over stored embryos, not a court's resolution of a dispute over embryo disposition where no such agreement exists; that broader topic was not researched for this clause and is outside what this clause covers.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — DONOR PARENTAGE INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Intended Parent, Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Intended Parent, Pat Morgan: ☐ _________________________ (if applicable)

Signature of Donor, Taylor Morgan: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside, and not as a substitute for, an actual written agreement described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613, or one of the optional California Statutory Forms for Assisted Reproduction described in Cal. Fam. Code § 7613.5. It does not itself establish, or fail to establish, any party's parentage of a child conceived through assisted reproduction; that outcome is determined by which provision of § 7613 applies to the facts as they occurred. Unlike this corpus's separate Gestational Carrier (Surrogacy) Agreement Information Sheet, nothing in the text of Cal. Fam. Code § 7613 requires that signatures on a donor written agreement be notarized or witnessed, though the optional statutory forms under § 7613.5 each include their own notary acknowledgment block for parties who choose to use one of them.]

expectedJSON.body: Family Code § 7613 also addresses, within its own text, the parentage of the intended parent who is not the donor and not the person who conceives and gives birth. Under § 7613(a)(1), if a woman conceives through assisted reproduction using semen or ova, or both, donated by a donor who is not the woman's spouse, and does so "with the consent of another intended parent," that other intended parent "is treated in law as if that intended parent is the natural parent of a child thereby conceived." That consent "shall be in writing and signed by the other intended parent and the woman conceiving through assisted reproduction." Under § 7613(a)(2), the absence of a signed writing does not automatically defeat that intended parent's status: a court may still find the intended parent consented if it finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that before conception the woman and the intended parent had an oral agreement that both would be parents of the child. Nothing in the text of § 7613(a) conditions this outcome on the parties' marital status, on the intended parent's or woman's sex or gender, or on the involvement of a licensed physician.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code § 7613.5 is a separate, companion statutory section that supplies optional fill-in forms for use alongside § 7613, not a different substantive parentage rule. Section 7613.5(a) states that "an intended parent may, but is not required to, use the forms set forth in this section to demonstrate the intent to be a legal parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction," and that "these forms shall satisfy the writing requirement specified in Section 7613," while also making clear that the forms "do not affect any presumptions of parentage based on Section 7611, and do not preclude a court from considering any other claims to parentage under California statute or case law." Section 7613.5(d) confirms use of these particular forms is optional: "this section does not require the use of one of these forms to satisfy the writing requirement of Section 7613" — a different written agreement can also satisfy § 7613's own writing elements. Critically for how this framework relates to this corpus's separate Gestational Carrier (Surrogacy) Agreement Information Sheet, § 7613.5(c) states directly that "these forms do not apply to assisted reproduction agreements for gestational carriers or surrogacy agreements." Sections 7613 and 7613.5 (governing a donor or genetic-material provider's own parentage, and an intended parent's consent-based parentage, outside a gestational-carrier arrangement) and Family Code §§ 7960-7962 (governing an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers specifically) are two distinct, parallel statutory frameworks within the same Uniform Parentage Act part of the Family Code, addressing different fact patterns: this framework does not itself impose, and its text does not cross-reference, the independent-counsel, notarization-or-witnessing, or pre-embryo-transfer-execution requirements that § 7962 imposes specifically on gestational carrier agreements, and conversely the optional § 7613.5 forms are, by their own terms, unusable for a gestational carrier or surrogacy agreement.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code § 7613 addresses two further, more specific situations beyond the core donor and provider rules described elsewhere in this document. First, § 7613(d)(2) addresses a chain-of-custody problem: "if the provider of ova, semen, or embryos is not the original source of the ova or sperm, each original provider's written consent to the donation is required unless that person has executed a writing to consent to the donation, or to waive or relinquish their right to the genetic material, or as otherwise ordered by a court of law." Second, § 7613(e) addresses a written renunciation agreement between two people who jointly control the disposition of stored embryos. Under § 7613(e)(1), if those two people "are not married to one another," they may enter a written agreement in which one of them "renounces all legal interest in the embryos, with the specific intent that the person renouncing all legal interest shall not be a legal parent of any child conceived with use of the embryos," and once that renunciation is signed by everyone with a legal interest in or control over the embryos, "the renouncing person shall be treated in law as a donor, and not a legal parent"; either party may then file the agreement with the court for "an order establishing the nonparentage of the donor." Under § 7613(e)(2), if the two people sharing control of the embryos are instead married to one another at the time they sign such an agreement, it does not become legally binding until "the court's entry of a final decree of dissolution that incorporates the agreement," after which specified marital-presumption provisions (Family Code § 7540, and § 7611(a)-(c)) no longer apply.
